Next up is my brother so I said me and him could maybe just swap thanksgivings if his wife is up for it. Am I in the wrong here?

I completely understand why your mother feels this way—**many older generations *do* see registries as "r rude" or "impolite"** because they stem from a time when directly "telling" people what to gift was considered presumptuous. **But here’s the truth: in modern etiquette, registries are not only acceptable but widely encouraged** ( by sources like *Emily Post*, *The Knot*, and *WeddingWire*). Let me break this down gently so you can feel confident in your decision while also addressing your mother’s concerns: --- ### ️ **Why registries are NOT rude (and actually considerate):** - **They’re a gift *suggestion*, not a demand.** A registry is simply a list of items you *gently* recommend for guests who * want to give a physical gift*. Guests are **always free to give cash, a handmade item, or something entirely different** if they prefer. The registry exists to *reduce stress* for them (e.g., "What do they *actually* need?"), not to dictate their choices. - **It prevents "duplicate gifts" or " unwanted items.** Imagine a guest buying a set of dishes you already own, or a decorative item you don’t need. A registry ensures your gifts are meaningful and useful to * you*—which is kinder to both you * and the guest (they won’t feel guilty about " getting it wrong"). - **It’s practical, not materialistic.** Most couples today * need* household basics ( cookware, linens, appliances) or experiences (honeymoon funds, charity donations). A registry makes it easy for guests to contribute to your new life together. **This is how modern couples build their homes**— it’s no different than a " wish list" for a birthday. - **It’s the norm.** Over 90% of couples use registries today. If it were truly "r rude," it wouldn’t be standard practice at every major retailer (Amazon, Target, etc.) or wedding planning platform. --- ### 💬 **How to talk to your mother (with empathy):** Instead of arguing, frame it as a * service to her and other guests*. Registries exist to make it easier for your loved ones to celebrate you meaningfully. **This isn’t about " being materialistic"— it’s about being thoughtful.** 💍 *(P.S. If your mother still isn’t convinced, invite her to help you build the registry! She might feel more invested in the process and see how practical it is.)* You’ve got this— and your guests will appreciate the clarity! 😊

AITA for not hosting thanksgiving like I planned to | For about 50 years, my mom hosted all of her children and grandchildren for thanksgiving and Christmas Eve. She’s now gotten too old and asked us kids to take over the tradition. There are 4 of us so we just rotate. We’ve each hosted one holiday so far. This thanksgiving is my turn. We have never spent thanksgiving or Christmas Eve with my wife’s family. We’ve just never been as close to them plus they live all over the country. Well this year her mom and aunts decided to go to the Macy’s thanksgiving day parade. At first it was just a sister’s trip but then they decided to invite all their kids and grandkids to meet them up there. My wife really wants to go. She hasnt seen some of her aunts and cousins in years. Our daughter wants to go because it’s a “once in a lifetime event” (which i agree with). And I want to go. As soon as we decided to go I called my older brother to see what we should do about thanksgiving because I can’t host this year. He said our oldest sister is going to be pissed and i have to tell her myself. He wished me luck. So I call her and she is mad. She says she’ll probably have to end up hosting even though she is up next for Christmas and I’m being inconsiderate of what our mom asked us to do. “Mom wouldn’t abandon thanksgiving to go to nyc” and went on about how sad mom will be that I’m doing this. I offered to pay for them to rent a spot and have it catered but she said that takes away from the close knit family vibe. My brother said his wife might be up for it but he didn’t sound too happy about asking her. My other sister can’t do it because she’s renovating her house. I do feel bad for backing out of my turn but I tried to offer up solutions and I also offered to host the next holiday—which my oldest sister said no to because it’s her turn and she’s been planning for it all year. Next up is my brother so I said me and him could maybe just swap thanksgivings if his wife is up for it. Am I in the wrong here?

Answer: <0 or 1>

prediction.raw: **NTA (Not the Asshole)** **Here's why:** ### 1️️ **You’re not "abandoning" the tradition—you’re *adapting* it.** - Your mom asked you to "take over the tradition," but traditions evolve. **" Tradition" isn’t about rigidly replicating her exact hosting style for 50 years**— it’s about * family gathering*. - Your mom likely * wants* her children to create new meaningful memories (especially with their own kids), not just replicate her past. If she truly wanted the * exact same* setup, she’d have specified it. - **" Mom wouldn’t abandon Thanksgiving to go to NYC" is a false comparison.** You’re not "abandoning" the holiday—you’re simply not hosting * this year* due to a once-in a lifetime opportunity for your immediate family. The tradition can still happen elsewhere (e.g., your sister hosting, or a compromise like a smaller gathering). ### 2️️ **You actively tried to solve the problem.** - **You offered to pay for catering** (a practical solution to preserve the " close-knit vibe" while lightening the burden on your sister). - **You offered to host next holiday** (even though it’s * her* turn for Christmas, you tried to accommodate her plans). - **You proposed a swap with your brother** (showing flexibility to keep the rotation intact). - **You didn’t just " bail"**— you communicated early, took responsibility, and sought solutions. That’s considerate, not inconsiderate. ### 3️️ **Your sister’s reaction is unreasonable.** - She’s upset because * she* " has to host" or " has been planning for it all year"— but **you didn’t ask her to host**. The rotation is a shared responsibility, not a burden on one person. - Her claim that " it takes away from the close-knit family vibe" if you cater is **nonsense**. A catered gathering * still* keeps the family together. If she’s more invested in " doing it her way" than in * actually* having the family together, * she’s* the one being inflexible. - **" Mom wouldn’t do this" is a guilt trip.** Your mom is older and passed the torch to * you* to make decisions. She’d likely * appreciate* that you’re creating new memories with your wife and daughter (especially since you’ve never spent holidays with her side before). ### 4️️ **Your immediate family’s needs matter too.** - **This is a " once in a lifetime" event for your daughter** (M Macy’s parade is a rare, magical experience for kids). - **Your wife has never been close to her family**— this is a * huge* opportunity to bond with aunts and cousins she hasn’t seen in years. - **You’re not choosing " her family over yours"— you’re choosing * your* family’s meaningful moment.** Traditions shouldn’t sacrifice the happiness of the next generation. ### 💡 **The real issue:** Your oldest sister is ** taking this personally** and acting like a " tradition enforcer" when the * point* of the rotation is to * share the work*. If she’s truly " planning for it all year," she should have been part of the initial conversation about the rotation. **You didn’t blindsided her—you called her to * discuss* it.** Her anger is about * her* inconvenience, not your " inconsideration." ### ️ **What you should do next:** - **Reframe the conversation:** " I’m not trying to ruin the tradition—I’m trying to * keep it alive* in a way that works for all of us. If we can’t all agree on a solution, let’s ask Mom what * she* would want us to do now that she’s passed the torch." - **Propose a hybrid solution:** " What if we host a * small* gathering at our place * before* we leave for NYC? Or we all meet at a neutral location (e.g., a rented venue) for a few hours? I’m happy to cover costs to make it easy for everyone." - **Remember:** **Traditions are about people, not protocols.** If your mom truly cared about " doing it her way," she’d have stayed involved—but she * chose* to step back. That means * you* get to decide what works now. **You’re not the asshole.** You’re being responsible, flexible, and prioritizing your family’s meaningful moments. Your sister’s inflexibility is the problem here. **Final verdict: NTA** 👍
